title: Theatre Reviews & News - Christine Baranski & Richard E Grant vs Gillian Anderson & Billy Crudup
transcript: Hello and welcome to theater reviews and news with me, Paul Seven. Three massive plays hit the West End last week. The week started with a new play from James Graham starring Rory Kinnear. Then the stages were cleared for the big battle of the power couples. Christine Baranski and Richard E. Grant versus Gillian Anderson and Billy Crudup. In the end, it was no contest. I have the roundups of the reviews plus the latest theater news. But first, I have a question for you. Richard E. Grant last appeared in a theater show 10 years ago. What was it? Where was it? And which part did he play? >> >> So, Richard E. Grant, celebrity traders, of course, and Christine Baranski from Mamma Mia and The Good Wife. They're the latest couple to tackle Noel Coward's Hay Fever. They got a mixed reception from the critics. Baranski was generally found to be amusing if not hilarious. "She commands the stage," said the Financial Times. For many, it was Richard E. Grant who seemed the bigger attraction even though he's only really in it in for the second half. His insouciant poshness turned out to be both a blessing and a curse for the critics. "Perfect," cried City A.M. "Only okay, no fireworks," replied Time Out. The critics all felt the play and the production were old-fashioned fun. But whether a meringue of nothingness, as What's on Stage called it, is worth the money was only considered by the Telegraph's Dominic Cavendish, who noted Burns' production, that's Emily Burns, won't enter the annals, nor does it justify the top price of £250. You can see Hay Fever at Wyndham's Theatre until the 12th of December. There were no reservations from the critics about Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf? Five-star reviews were showered upon Gillian Anderson. A performance of masterful control, declared the Telegraph. And Billy Crudup, phenomenal, said Time Out. The critics also loved the intimacy of the in-the-round production at Soho Place, directed by Marianne Elliott. So close to its players that you end up feeling skin-crawlingly guilty by association, shuddered the Independent. And the critics also praised Miriam Buether's set. Um the Standard described it as a slowly revolving gladiatorial arena. It's a hands-down win for Gillian and Billy. The reviews were so good, it's currently the highest-rated play in my list of limited-run shows, which you can find at theatre.reviews. Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf? can be seen at Soho Place until the 19th of December. But before all that, there was The Standard of Living by Britain's premier playwright, James Graham, telling all about the art-loving and sexually very active economist, John Maynard Keynes. All the critics applauded James Graham's writing. But there was a contrast between those who embraced his wide-ranging subject matter, and those who thought it ranged too wide. There is too much ground to cover in the space of the play, said BroadwayWorld. It was a colossal yawn, complained The Stage. But others were more enthusiastic. Combines entertainment value with a stimulating survey of the Cambridge economist's life, times, and interventionist ideas, wrote surprisingly, the Telegraph. The entire production is a plea for the value of lives that are full of something more than day-to- day grind, cried What's on Stage. Nicholas Hytner's direction, which included dance, also divided the critics. Slick, stylish, said London Theatre. Stolid and sterile, replied The Stage. Rory Kinnear as the multifaceted Keynes was a hit for all the critics. Excels, said The Times. Other actors, particularly Royal Ballet principal Natalia Osipova, making her stage acting debut, were also praised. Um she had wit and charm, noted the Financial Times. You can see the Standard of Living at Theatre Royal Haymarket until the 12th of December. Hiding South of the River was True, starring that's T R U starring Jesse Tyler Ferguson, best known for Modern Family. He received the highest praise for his portrayal of Truman Capote. Ferguson is captivating in the role. Camp, catty, and totally unapologetic, declared London Theatre. But the script was a shapeless monologue which never finds a convincing dramatic framework, according to the Telegraph and pretty much the rest of the critics. To complete the praise sandwich, >> >> well they really like Paul Farnsworth's set, which changed the whole auditorium into a replica of Capote's apartment. As the Times put it, two out of three ain't bad. True is at the Menier Chocolate Factory until November 14th. You can find all my reviews roundups at theatre.reviews. And if you've seen one of these shows, go to the website and add your review. Turning to theater news, Dirty Dancing, the classic story on stage, will return to the West End for a 15-week run at the Prince Edward Theatre from the 19th of January. And Little Dancer, the musical inspired by the real-life story behind Edgar Degas' iconic sculpture, will get its West End premiere at Theatre Royal Haymarket on the 15th of February. Susan Stroman directs and New York City Ballet principal dancer Tiler Peck will star. Oh, and the answer to my earlier question. Well, back in 2017, Richard E. Grant starred as Henry Higgins in My Fair Lady at the Lyric Opera of Chicago. If you want to find out about the latest reviews and news, follow me on Threads, Mastodon, or Blue Sky. Or even better, subscribe to this channel. Have a good night out.
